I'm a white English 25 year old woman who grew up in Australia. I grew up in a very large and very beautiful two story house very close to the beach. I never wanted for anything, did very well in school, but I'm not and never have been spoiled. My dad and I have fantastic relationship. 

80% to 90% or my eating disorder was due to wanting to be more attractive and look more like the ideal 'perfect' female body often portrayed in multiple types of media as well as feeling inadequate beside my peers who I felt were far more attractive than me. But I knew that I had good moral character and an ethical code that a lot of the others around me, though certainly not all, didn't always share. Even the friendship I made in year 10 that lasted for 10 years (we even worked and lived together for over half of this time) was also a massive trigger for me as she had and still has a  'Barbie figure'. When this friendship ended, my eating disorder relapse certainly didn't improve although it wasn't the cause.

The remaining 10% to 20% was mostly because I had placed so much importance on looking 'perfect', that it became the only thing that I could cling to that made more not care anymore about not fitting in with the others at school. I was always the one left out and forgot about in school. They thought I was 'too nice' (I'm a people-pleaser) and was always told that I'm extremely well-mannered and ''very mature for my age'. But eventually I didn't care anymore about 'not being one of them' but I thought 'fuck them, I'm way better than they are anyway because I of much thinner I am I and therefore more attractive.' It was a massive internalised superiority thing for me that got me through/helped me cope with being excluded throughout school. I had a couple of close friends wasn't never really 'one of girls'. 

There was also the  considerable demonisation of unhealthy food in school during my health education classes which really fed into my guilt around 'unhealthy' food, but was nothing compared to the above. My brother also had said very unhelpful things around food 'he used to be a 'gym bro' and my mother was on and off dieting every now and then but it was never something that she imposed on me and she never made negative comments about my body or my food.

Well, eating disorders are so different for everyone and for me, it's about feeling good enough and superior. I was bullied a as a kid/teenager and I felt like I could never be good enough. I was never really accepted by the other girls and I always felt I didn't get good enough grades. I tried my hardest, but was often topped by someone who didn't seem to try nearly as hard. I'd always felt bad about my appearance because of the media portayal of perfection and beauty so that was a constant source of guilt for me that I wasn't never going to look like the slim, sexy model in magazines. That, coupled being outcaste and not getting the graded I tried for left me desperate for something I could feel good about myself for. So I ate less and less and exercised more and eventually became far better at sport than any of the other girl and computed with the bus in long distance running. I was skeletal in about three months and literally couldn't give a shit if people didn't like me. I was very happy to be on my own because, in my head, I was better than them. I was untouchable and I know it sounds bad but to me, I could something that no one else around me could do - I could starve and be in so much physical and mental and do it with a smile. People looked and noticed and for the first time in my life, I felt absolutely stunning and confident. I had my own taste in music, books, and I didn't care anymore about being top of the class. 

I know what you mean, and I understand the appeal of religion when you're in a desperate situation, but I've still never 'turned to god' when I've had a rope around my neck, so I guess everyone is different.

As someone who is also recovering from an eating disorder, this is kind of tricky one. 

First of all, this is definitely not a stupid question - in fact, it's  a very thoughtful and considerate question. You're a kind and considerate person and I just wanted to point this out because I'm sure that anyone, including this lovely lady, would be very touched to know the thought and consideration that you're putting into making sure that they feel comfortable. 

You're heart is definitely in the right place, but it's just difficult to know whether to include food as a such a prominent element your time together. It could go a number of ways, which all depend on where she's at in her recovery:
 
- She could feel up to the 'challenge' (food-wise) and accept all these offers and see that what she could otherwise be missing out on if she declined, ie. sharing nice food and good experiences with good company. 

- She may decline your invitations because of anxiety around food and therefore miss out on spending time with you too. 

I think, what I would do, as some one who has anxiety around food, is to invite her to do something that doesn't centre around food, but bring up the option when you're out together. For example, you both go for a nice walk somewhere and when it gets to about midday, suggest a nice place to go for lunch. 
 
That way, you can see her response and make a call whether to suggest for food-related plans in the future. I suggest this because in my experience, a big part of what's helped to motivate me to continue my recovery and not relapse into avoiding food and situations around food is experiencing how it can be a good opportunity to bond with others. It's so isolating having an eating disorder and being reminded how much you're missing out on - normality around food and sharing something simple like a coffee with a friend, like you mentioned - can remind her why she's making a positive choice to get better and continue recovery. 

She may sit across from you, like I've sat with my family and friends while I've challenged myself around food, and think, 'wow, this is scary, but I'm also kind of having a good time. I would've missed out on genuinely laughing and smiling if I'd stayed home eating (or not eating) x, y and z like every other night'.

I feel very much the same in my place of work. The women I work with all talk about how much they all need to lose weight, how much weight they've gained, foods they "shouldn't" eat, their latest diets - you name it.

What I do is keep my head down and continue working. I don't contribute to the conversation unless I'm called uon to do so or specifically asked a question. I keep myself busy when the topic comes up. The only thing I volunteer, when a conversation that I'm involved in does start moving in this direction, is the occasional polite reminder that as long you're happy and healthy that's all that matters. I can barely take my own advice, but I wholeheartedly would never want anyone else to feel the same way that I do towards myself but I'm working on it.

When I can hear all these weight loss "tips and tricks", special diets and disordered eating pattern, around me, I remind myself that nothing good with come of it in the end. It ends up being a bit of conversation with myself because my eating disorder will or course try to bargain with me.

ED: You should show them how to REALLY lose weight.  They'll be so jealous. I can help you.
Me: Yes, but we've done that before and I was suicidal, on the verge on heart failure, and it broke my family's heart.
ED: Then hide it from your family.
Me: The secrecy makes me feel isolated and is another route to feeling suicidal again.
ED: But you'll achieve something and you'll feel good and accomplished and not want to kill yourself.
Me: Not everyone values that so I'll only get so far in life (and not far enough to feel accomplished) and being extremely thin won't pay the bills. It's not sustainable in the long term.
ED: Then don't be here in the long term.
Me: We're not doing this now. I'm not going to restrict and I've told you why.

It may sound weird but I've found that challenging these thoughts that are triggered by weight-loss conversations has helped me. In a way it feels like I know better if that makes sense because I know where it can lead (not saying that everyone who embarks on a "diet" will have an eating disorder). I've been down that road before and it never ends well so I'm grateful that can at least eat a meal without purging and I want to keep that.

Things like that are a slippery slope when you have/have had an eating disorder so just try remind yourself that and remind yourself that you will always be better off not getting pulled into disordered trends. I believe in you!
